name: Irish republican legitimism
summary: Irish republican legitimism holds that the Irish Republic proclaimed in 1916 and set up by the First and Second Dail still exists in law, that the 1921 Treaty and the two states that followed it have no lawful authority, and that the Second Dail passed its powers in 1938 to the IRA Army Council. Its adherents therefore refuse to recognise or sit in the parliaments, courts and police of the 26-county and 6-county states, and claim the right to resist foreign rule by arms. The strand that carries the doctrine today, Republican Sinn Fein, pairs it with a federal, decentralised, democratic socialist programme for a 32-county Ireland.
scope: The legitimist strand of Irish republicanism: the doctrine of legal continuity of the Republic (1916 Proclamation, 1919 First Dail, 1921 Second Dail, 1938 handover to the Army Council) and the abstentionist and anti-partition positions drawn from it, as set out by Ruairi O Bradaigh's wing that left Sinn Fein in 1986 and by Republican Sinn Fein, which the defining sources name as legitimism's carrier. Answers rest on the doctrine's own statements plus Republican Sinn Fein's published programmes (Eire Nua, Saol Nua, the 2007 manifesto). It excludes Provisional Sinn Fein after 1986 and republicans who do not claim the Second Dail succession, and no general Irish republican source is used. Its positions on topics outside these programmes are left null.

missingStatements.text: A nation's independence is not a matter for a vote.
missingStatements.rationale: The legitimists hold that national sovereignty is inalienable and not open to reconsideration, and that no vote of one generation, including the 1998 referendums, can cancel it.

quotes.text: Ireland’s right to national freedom and independence is actually not a matter of a vote for any single generation
quotes.where: Des Dalton, The Irish Times, 26 March 2016

quotes.text: the sovereignty and unity of the republic are inalienable and non-renunciable. In other words, they can’t be given away and are not a matter for reconsideration.
quotes.where: O Bradaigh speech, 2 November 1986, fifth paragraph

missingStatements.text: People should refuse to recognise the courts of a state they regard as illegitimate.
missingStatements.rationale: Republican Sinn Fein rejects the courts and laws of both Irish states and counts every court of the Oireachtas as illegitimate; O Bradaigh allowed court appearances only as a tactic.

quotes.text: In particular we reject English police, English courts, English laws in Ireland.
every law enacted by the Oireachtas, the president, the courts, the Garda Síochána, the Defence Forces, all public servants – all count for nothing because all are illegitimate.
quotes.where: Irish Times, 26 March 2016, section Institutional development

notes: Themes searched: doctrine and abstention (Walsh, O Luain, O Bradaigh, Lynn 2001 read but not cited because it never names the term), constitution and federalism (Eire Nua), economy, ecology, culture and foreign policy (Saol Nua), violence and courts (Dalton; the IRA Green Book's legitimacy note was read but not cited because no defining source names it). Not found: published legitimist positions on immigration, drugs, policing detail, criminal justice, gender and family law, nuclear power, climate, the monarchy beyond the republic itself, and most of the 'means' and 'society' statements. The doctrine itself (Second Dail succession) is narrow; most answers come from the programmes of Republican Sinn Fein, the party the defining sources tie to it, and other groups claiming the same lineage (Continuity IRA, 32 County Sovereignty Movement, Eirigi) are not separately covered.
